questions.stem: In a review problem, for an iron system with internal energy change 139 kJ and entropy change -15 J per K held at constant volume, compute the Helmholtz free energy change at 285 K in kJ.

options.misconception: Did not convert entropy units to kJ
Added the T delta S term instead of subtracting
Correct application of the principle
Ignored entropy and reported internal energy alone

questions.explanation: Helmholtz free energy is defined as A equals U minus T S, so its change at constant temperature is delta U minus T delta S. With entropy in J per K converted to kJ per K, the value at 285 K is 143.28 kJ; its decrease sets the maximum work obtainable at constant volume and temperature.
questions.hint: Delta A = delta U - T delta S.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Maximum Non-Expansion Work principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a skills drill, an iron process at constant temperature and pressure has delta H 82 kJ and delta S -17 J per K at 457 K; find the maximum non-expansion work in kJ.

options.misconception: Used enthalpy change instead of free energy
Correct application of the principle
Used the negative of enthalpy instead of free energy
Used delta G itself instead of its negative

questions.explanation: At constant temperature and pressure the maximum useful non-expansion work equals minus the change in Gibbs free energy. Computing delta G as delta H minus T delta S gives 89.77 kJ, so the maximum non-expansion work is -89.77 kJ; a negative delta G corresponds to positive work available.
questions.hint: Maximum non-PV work = -delta G.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Otto Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a skills drill, with iron cylinder walls, compression ratio 7, and inlet temperature 319 K, an ideal Otto cycle at gamma 1.4 runs; compute its air-standard thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Used a simple one minus reciprocal ratio expression
Correct application of the principle
Reported the reciprocal term without subtracting it
Used gamma instead of gamma minus one in the exponent

questions.explanation: The ideal Otto efficiency is one minus one over the compression ratio raised to gamma minus one. With compression ratio 7 and gamma 1.4 the exponent is 0.4, giving 54.1 percent; raising the compression ratio increases efficiency but is limited by knock in real engines.
questions.hint: Otto efficiency = 1 - 1/r^(gamma - 1).

questions.learningObjective: Apply Brayton Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a field measurement, with silver compressor blades, pressure ratio 4, and inlet temperature 314 K, an ideal Brayton cycle at gamma 1.4 runs; compute its thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Reported the pressure term itself without subtracting
Used gamma instead of (gamma minus one) over gamma
Flipped the sign of the pressure-ratio exponent
Correct application of the principle

questions.explanation: For an ideal Brayton cycle the efficiency depends on the pressure ratio as one minus rp raised to minus (gamma minus one) over gamma. With rp equal to 4 and gamma 1.4 this gives 32.7 percent; higher pressure ratios improve efficiency at the cost of heavier compressors.
questions.hint: Brayton efficiency = 1 - (1/rp)^((gamma-1)/gamma).

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Carnot Cycle Work principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a homework problem, a brass Carnot engine working between 733 K and 250 K absorbs 1216 J per cycle from the hot reservoir. Calculate the work output per cycle in joules.

options.misconception: Computed the heat rejected rather than the work
Reported the full absorbed heat as work
Correct application of the principle
Added the reservoir ratio to the absorbed heat

questions.explanation: A reversible Carnot engine converts a fraction (1 minus Tc over Th) of the absorbed heat into work. With reservoirs at 733 K and 250 K and heat input 1216 J, the work output is 801 J per cycle; the remainder is rejected to the cold reservoir.
questions.hint: Work = Q_in (1 - T_cold/T_hot) for a Carnot cycle.

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Compression-Ignition Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In an instrument check, at compression ratio 15 and cutoff ratio 2.54 with gamma 1.4, an ideal compression-ignition cycle with copper pistons runs. Compute its air-standard efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Reported only the cutoff correction, not one minus it
Correct application of the principle
Used the Otto cycle formula and ignored the cutoff ratio
Used gamma rather than gamma minus one

questions.explanation: The compression-ignition cycle efficiency equals one minus one over r to the gamma minus one times a cutoff-ratio factor (rho to the gamma minus one) over (gamma times rho minus one). With r 15 and rho 2.54 the efficiency is 57.8 percent; at a cutoff ratio of one it reduces to the Otto result.
questions.hint: Diesel-type efficiency = 1 - [1/r^(gamma-1)] [(rho^gamma - 1)/(gamma(rho - 1))].

questions.subject: THERMODYNAMICS
questions.learningObjective: Apply Rankine Cycle Efficiency principles to solve a quantitative thermodynamics problem.
questions.stem: In a calibration run, a steam Rankine plant with aluminum piping adds 1869 kJ per kg in the boiler and rejects 932 kJ per kg in the condenser. Evaluate the cycle thermal efficiency as a percentage.

options.misconception: Divided net work by the condenser rejection
Reported the rejected-heat fraction as efficiency
Correct application of the principle
Inverted the heat-addition-to-rejection ratio

questions.explanation: Thermal efficiency of any power cycle is net work divided by heat input, which for a Rankine plant is (Qin minus Qout) over Qin. Substituting 1869 and 932 kJ per kg gives 50.1 percent; the condenser rejection is a necessary loss, not part of the useful output.
questions.hint: Efficiency = (Q_boiler - Q_condenser) / Q_boiler.
